extraction.name: TOFU : A Task of Fictitious Unleaming for LLMs
extraction.description: We present TOFU, a Task of Fictitious Unleaming, as a benchmark aimed at helping deepen our understanding of unleaming. We offer a dataset of 200 diverse synthetic author profiles, each consisting of 20 question-answer pairs, and a subset of these profiles called the forget set that serves as the target for unleaming.
extraction.creator: Pratyush Maini, Zhili Feng, Avi Schwarzschild, Zachary C. Lipton, J. Zico Kolter
extraction.citeAs: TOFU : A Task of Fictitious Unleaming for LLMs
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is composed entirely of fictitious author biographies, synthesized by GPT-4. It is crafted by prompting GPT-4 to generate data about each author based on predefined attributes (birthplace, gender, birth year, writing genre, awards received, parents’ professions). Each author profile consists of 20 question-answer pairs.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The fictitious author biographies are synthesized by GPT-4. To seed names for book titles, the Goodreads Books dataset available on Kaggle was used.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset is split into a 'forget set' (target for unleaming) and a 'retain set'. Three splits are provided: 90-10, 95-5, and 99-1. Initial data generation with a generic prompt showed biases (e.g., author birth years between 1970-1980, specific book title words like ‘echoes’, ‘shadows’, ‘tides’, ‘whispers’, similar upbringings, ‘magical’ writing style). To minimize these biases, an elaborate prompt was used to deterministically seed various author attributes (place/time of birth, gender orientation, genre, parents' occupation, book title keywords from Goodreads Books dataset).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: GPT-4 was prompted to generate 20 question-answer pairs for each fictitious author. For evaluation metrics, GPT-4 was also used to paraphrase answers and generate five factually incorrect perturbed answers for the Truth Ratio metric.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 20 question-answer pairs per fictitious author profile.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes attributes for fictitious authors such as birthplace, gender, birth year, and parents’ professions. While fictitious, these attributes are typically considered sensitive if they pertained to real individuals.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to help develop unleaming methods that imbue AI systems with privacy, critical for safe and legal deployment, especially in light of regulations like the Right to be Forgotten. It addresses concerns about LLMs memorizing and reproducing sensitive or private data.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Initial data generation with a generic prompt for GPT-4 resulted in biases: most author birth years were concentrated in 1975 (between 1970-1980, particularly August), book titles frequently contained words like ‘echoes’, ‘shadows’, ‘tides’, and ‘whispers’, and authors had similar upbringings and ‘magical’ writing styles. These biases were mitigated by using an elaborate prompt to deterministically seed diverse author attributes.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark focuses on entity-level forgetting (forgetting everything about a person) and does not cover instance-level unleaming (forgetting a specific answer about a person), behavior-level unleaming (alignment to human values), or in-context unleaming. It is designed for unleaming information learned during finetuning, not pretraining. The measure of indistinguishability is an approximation, not a full (ε,δ)-unleaming condition, and models outputting gibberish can falsely indicate strong forget quality if not paired with model utility. The scope of benchmarked unleaming methods is limited to popular but simple algorithms. The compute constraint for unleaming algorithms (O(number of samples)) might not be optimal for real-world scenarios involving tiny forget sets from huge pretraining corpora.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed as a benchmark for evaluating and understanding machine unleaming methods for Large Language Models (LLMs). It is used for finetuning base LLMs and then for evaluating their ability to 'forget' specific fictitious authors (forget set) while retaining performance on other data (retain set, real authors, world facts). It serves as a task for training, testing, and validation of unleaming algorithms.
